newsitem.title: USA: Cisco earnings rose 34 percent, matching forecasts.
newsitem.headline: Cisco earnings rose 34 percent, matching forecasts.

text.p: Cisco Systems Inc. said Tuesday that profit from operations rose 34 percent in the latest quarter, matching Wall Street forecasts, on slightly weaker-than-expected revenue.

"This came in precisely as we expected on earnings and revenue," said Noel Lindsey, analyst at investment bank Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "Yet at the same time we were hoping that they would be on the upside (as they are) when times are good."
The results were released after the market closed. Cisco shares had risen 31.3 cents to $81.938 on Nasdaq, but slipped to as low as $79.75 in after-hours trading.

The world's biggest maker of computer networking gear reported profit from operations of $383 million, or 55 cents a share, for its fourth quarter, compared with profit from operations of $286 million, or 42 cents a share, a year earlier.

With charges for two acquisitions and a gain from the sale of an investment, the company reported net income of $151 million, or 22 cents a share, for the latest quarter ended July 26. That compared with net profits of $276.6 million, or 41 cents a share, in the 1996 period.
Wall Street expected Cisco, based in San Jose, Calif., to report operating earnings of 55 cents a share, according to Zacks Investment Research, which tracks analysts' estimates.
Sales rose 37 percent to $1.77 billion from $1.29 billion.

Cisco gained market share in all its product lines, which are used to link computers into networks, the company said. Sales, however, came in on the lower side of the $1.76 billion to $1.8 billion Wall Street analysts had expected.
Sales were hurt by weak economies in Japan, France and Germany, said Cisco Chief Executive John Chamber.
"In the U.S., 43 percent of the spending in the economy is on high-tech," Chamber said. "Where your economy gets into trouble, people will spend less on high-tech."
He said, however, he expects sales to pick up around the winter quarter as the company rolls out a new line of high-end routers, the main workhorse of a corporate computer network.
